title: Burke Impeaches Warren Hastings
speaker: Edmund Burke
before: Warren Hastings had governed Bengal for the East India Company from 1773 and came home in 1785 to charges of misconduct and corruption, pressed by Philip Francis and the opposition Whigs. His trial before the House of Lords opened in Westminster Hall on 13 February 1788, and Edmund Burke, leading the prosecution for the Commons, took four days to lay out the charges.
excerpt: I impeach him in the name of the people of India, whose laws, rights and liberties he has subverted; whose properties he has destroyed; whose country he has laid waste and desolate.
source: Burke's opening speech in the passages that The World's Famous Orations (1906) printed, ending with its close.
after: The trial sat on and off for seven years while public interest waned. On 23 April 1795 the Lords cleared Hastings by large majorities on every question put to them. The defence had cost him an estimated £71,000 of his own money, and Burke remained convinced of his guilt until his death in 1797.
notes: The World's Famous Orations prints extracts, not the whole of the four days: paragraphs on arbitrary power (Hastings's 'principles' of government), then the close with the 'I impeach him' sentences. It is the whole of what this public-domain source gives. Led: Cornwallis, whose testimony of 1794 lifted the defence (the article). Flag: 'World's Famous Orations' is the source's name, not in the article.

title: Jefferson's First Inaugural Address
speaker: Thomas Jefferson
place: Senate chamber, United States Capitol, Washington
before: Thomas Jefferson, vice president under John Adams, ran against him in the election of 1800 and tied with Aaron Burr in the Electoral College; the House of Representatives chose Jefferson on the 36th ballot. At the first inauguration held in Washington he walked to the Capitol and spoke in the Senate chamber, his theme reconciliation after a bitterly partisan election.
excerpt: But every difference of opinion is not a difference of principle. We have called by different names brethren of the same principle. We are all Republicans, we are all Federalists.
source: Jefferson's own text, of which he gave a copy to the National Intelligencer to publish as soon as he had delivered it.
after: Chief Justice John Marshall then gave him the oath of office. Adams had left Washington by the early stagecoach at four that morning, the first outgoing president not to attend his successor's inauguration, and power passed peaceably from one party to its rival after a free election.
notes: No led: the saved article says nothing of what followed beyond the oath and Adams's absence. The imported text has 'long- lost' (a line-break hyphen of the transcription) in its second paragraph: a $FIXES pair 'long- lost' -> 'long-lost' would mend it.

title: Robert Emmet's Speech from the Dock
speaker: Robert Emmet
empire: /empire/united-kingdom-of-great-britain-and-ireland|United Kingdom of Great Britain and Ireland
before: Robert Emmet, a Protestant United Irishman, led a rising in Dublin on 23 July 1803 that was to seize Dublin Castle and break the recent union with Great Britain; it misfired within hours. Captured on 25 August, he was tried for high treason on 19 September, called no witnesses, and spoke from the dock after the verdict, before sentence was passed.
excerpt: Let no man write my epitaph: for as no man who knows my motives dare now vindicate them, let not prejudice or ignorance asperse them.
source: As printed in The World's Famous Orations (1906). The text survives in many differing versions (Patrick Geoghegan counts over seventy); an early printing of 1818 drew on the notes of his counsel, Peter Burrowes.
after: Lord Norbury sentenced him to be hanged, drawn and quartered, and on 20 September he was hanged in Thomas Street and beheaded. Castlereagh wanted the rising treated as a contemptible insurrection, but it and the speech were taken up by the Young Irelanders, the Fenians and Patrick Pearse, who proclaimed a provisional government in Dublin in 1916.
notes: Which printing: The World's Famous Orations (1906), chosen because it names its book; it gives the speech without Lord Norbury's interruptions. Wikisource also has 'Speech from the Dock (Emmet)', from an Office of Public Works (Dublin) publication of uncertain date, which prints Norbury's interruptions; its close reads 'Let them and me rest in obscurity and peace', where the 1906 text has 'repose', and the 1818 printing quoted in the article differs again. The 1906 text has a stray full stop in its last paragraph ('character; when. my country'): a $FIXES pair 'character; when. my' -> 'character; when my' would mend it. Flag: 'World's Famous Orations' is the source's name.

title: Napoleon's Farewell to the Old Guard
speaker: Napoleon
before: The armies of the Sixth Coalition had taken Paris and the French Senate had dethroned Napoleon. He abdicated at the Palace of Fontainebleau, and the treaty signed on 11 April 1814 sent him into exile on Elba, with 400 men as his guard. Before he left, he took leave of the soldiers of his Old Guard.
excerpt: Soldiers, I bid you farewell. For twenty years that we have been together your conduct has left me nothing to desire.
source: As printed in English in The World's Famous Orations (1906), which names no translator.
after: Napoleon went into exile on Elba, which the treaty made a principality for him to rule. He escaped in 1815 and the Guard was raised again; at Waterloo the Old Guard held its formation and covered the retreat of the army before it was almost annihilated.
notes: Display is 'April 1814', not the brief's 20 April: neither saved article (Treaty of Fontainebleau, Imperial Guard) nor the text gives the day of the farewell. The 1906 text has 'I have always found you On the road to glory' (capital O, a slip of the transcription). Flag: 'World's Famous Orations' is the source's name.

title: Webster's Second Reply to Hayne
speaker: Daniel Webster
before: A Senate debate in January 1830 on a resolution of Samuel A. Foot to limit sales of public lands widened into a contest over nullification and the Union. Robert Y. Hayne of South Carolina, in a two-day speech, praised his state and attacked New England; Daniel Webster of Massachusetts rose the next day to reply, after a single night to prepare.
excerpt: It is, Sir, the people's Constitution, the people's government, made for the people, made by the people, and answerable to the people.
source: From The Great Speeches and Orations of Daniel Webster (1879). Webster's allies saw his preferred version of the speech into print soon after the debate.
after: Massachusetts men answered the speech with letters and public resolutions and had it widely printed. Its last words, "Liberty and Union, now and for ever, one and inseparable", became the motto of North Dakota, and Abraham Lincoln echoed "made for the people, made by the people" in the Gettysburg Address.
notes: Full text (30,215 words): paragraphs 4-146 of the page, the speech of 26-27 January 1830; left out are the editor's introduction and Webster's short answer to Hayne's rejoinder, which the page prints after it. Flag: 'Great Speeches and Orations' is the source's name. Robert Y. Hayne, Samuel Foot and the nullification crisis have no entries.

title: Black Hawk's Surrender Speech
speaker: Black Hawk
before: In April 1832 Black Hawk led more than 1,500 Sauk, Meskwaki and Kickapoo, warriors and families, into Illinois to reclaim land ceded under a disputed treaty of 1804. Militia and soldiers hunted the band down, and at the Bad Axe River most were killed or captured. On 27 August he surrendered at Prairie du Chien to the Indian agent Joseph Street.
excerpt: He has fought the battles of his country against the white man, who came year after year to cheat his people and take away their lands.
source: Black Hawk spoke in Sauk; the words reach us only in English, as Frank E. Stevens printed them in The Black Hawk War (1903), saying Black Hawk "is reported" to have spoken so.
after: Colonel Zachary Taylor took the prisoners into custody and sent them to Jefferson Barracks. In 1833 Black Hawk was taken east, met President Andrew Jackson and drew large crowds; before his release he told his life story to the interpreter Antoine LeClaire, and it was published that year.
full: https://www.gutenberg.org/cache/epub/49402/pg49402-images.html|Project Gutenberg, Frank E. Stevens, The Black Hawk War (1903)
notes: Text: one paragraph of Stevens (1903), who introduces it with 'he is reported to have addressed the latter as follows' and cites in his footnote 247 Fulton's Red Men of Iowa, p. 210 (not in the saved articles, so left out of the record). Nothing in the saved articles discusses this speech or who interpreted it; the source line says only what Stevens says, and the speech's authenticity deserves the editor's caution. Not found in Benjamin Drake's Life of Black Hawk (Gutenberg 18290), Thatcher's Indian Biography (1836) or McKenney and Hall. Flag: 'Frank E. Stevens' is the source's name. No entry for the Black Hawk War, the Battle of Bad Axe or Zachary Taylor.

title: Lamartine Refuses the Red Flag
speaker: Alphonse de Lamartine
before: The February Revolution of 1848 brought down Louis Philippe's monarchy. Alphonse de Lamartine, poet and deputy, announced a provisional government, and in the early hours of 25 February he proclaimed the Republic from the balcony of the Hôtel de Ville. That day, as part of the crowd there pressed for the red flag, Lamartine, now Foreign Minister, spoke for the tricolour.
excerpt: The government, I know, is as decided as myself, to die rather than to dishonor itself by obeying you.
source: From Lamartine's own History of the French Revolution of 1848, in which he writes of himself in the third person, tr. Francis A. Durivage and William S. Chase (Boston, 1849).
after: The tricolour remained the flag of France. Lamartine served as Foreign Minister until 11 May 1848 and then on the Executive Commission, but he lost the presidential election that year to Louis Napoleon Bonaparte and retired from political life. The revolution set off risings across Europe.
notes: DOUBTFUL TEXT: no transcription found on Wikisource or Gutenberg; the import is the OCR text of the Internet Archive scan (Boston: Phillips, Sampson, c1849; this copy 1851). Imported only the closing appeal (from 'Citizens, you can offer violence' to 'the liberty of the country'), 160 words; the earlier appeal ('Citizens, see what the sun of yesterday beheld ...') is broken in the OCR by a page header and OCR slips. The OCR keeps the printing's spaces before ; and ! and two line-break hyphens: $FIXES pairs 're- fuse' -> 'refuse' and 'tri- colored' -> 'tri-colored' (and, if wanted, ' ;' -> ';', ' !' -> '!') would mend them; the stronger passage, 'for the red flag which you offer us has only made the tour of the Champ de Mars ...', could replace my excerpt once fixed. title: Chief Seattle's Speech
speaker: Chief Seattle
before: Seattle, a leader of the Duwamish and Suquamish peoples who had sought cooperation with the American settlers, spoke in 1854 to Isaac Stevens, first governor of Washington Territory, on his visit to the town named after him. He spoke in Lushootseed, and his words most probably passed through Chinook Jargon before anyone put them into English.
excerpt: Every part of this country is sacred to my people. Every hill-side, every valley, every plain and grove has been hallowed by some fond memory or some sad experience of my tribe.
source: Henry A. Smith's reconstruction from his notes, printed 33 years later in the Seattle Sunday Star (1887): the exact words are not known, and Smith said he had recorded but a fragment.
after: Seattle was the first to sign the Treaty of Point Elliott in 1855, ceding about 2.5 million acres; many Duwamish renounced his leadership. He died on the Port Madison Reservation in 1866. Later versions, Clarence Bagley's of 1929 and those of William Arrowsmith and Ted Perry, added words of their own and made the speech an environmentalist credo.
notes: Imported: the speech only (paragraphs 7-15), without Smith's introduction and conclusion. The articles disagree on the year: Chief Seattle gives 1854, Chief Seattle's speech 'probably 1855'; 1854 kept as the brief says. The text carries the transcription's note marker '[1]' after 'Washington': a $FIXES pair 'Washington [1], can' -> 'Washington, can' would remove it. No entries for Isaac Stevens, the Duwamish, the Suquamish or the Treaty of Point Elliott, hence only two links (one the United States profile) and no led.
